How use(store) performs

With the React Compiler, use(store) matches or beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in 39 of 42 configurations of the main benchmark. It loses 3, all of them in one scenario: changing which row is selected, when every row reads the selection. For the losses in shared derived data, a recommended pattern wins in the same configurations. For selection, the recommended pattern wins every configuration where it was measured, in a separate sweep.

At a glance

Against the faster of Redux and Zustand, entity edits, adding or removing a row, and conditional reads win by wide margins: 2.4–9.2× faster, 2.9–7.8× faster, and 2.4–4.2× faster. Add / remove mostly measures list reconciliation (see caveats). Against them, the only scenario with losses is selection (see selection).

These are synthetic benchmarks with no data from a real app yet, and use(store) is an experiment that hasn't shipped (see caveats).

The headline is lower than the last report's: 39 of 42 configurations, against 36 of 36. A review fixed two places in the benchmark code that were unfair to the selector libraries, and the React build changed too. What changed has the details.

What the comparisons mean

The claim I'm testing: with the compiler, re-rendering only the components that read a changed store costs less than running every mounted selector on every update. Selector libraries like react-redux and Zustand subscribe each component with a selector. Every selector runs on every update to decide whether its component re-renders. use(store) has no selectors. A store update re-renders the components that read that store, and the compiler skips the parts of their output that didn't change.

The headline compares use(store) with the compiler against the faster of Redux and Zustand in each configuration, with each library at its own faster compiler setting. A configuration is one scenario at one list size and one CPU speed. The counting build that explains each result runs at 1,000 rows. The other comparisons are against each library on its own, against Context, and against a granular control (Zustand with a store per entity).

  • Editing one entity re-renders one row instead of running a selector in every row (2.4–9.2× faster). Adding or removing a row is 2.9–7.8× faster, and conditional reads are 2.4–4.2× faster.
  • It loses when the selection changes: 1.1× slower to 1.4× faster (1 faster, 2 tie, 3 slower). Every row reads the selected id, so every row re-renders, while selectors re-render only the two rows whose selection changed. The selection section explains why, and shows the pattern that wins.
  • The granular control has its own column (it isn't part of the headline). It puts each entity in its own Zustand store, to show how much of the win comes from granularity alone. use(store) loses 6 of 42 configurations to it, mostly on selection.

Two things aren't in the headline. Keyed selection, the recommended pattern for selection, is measured in the sweeps, not the main benchmark. The build without the same-element bailout has its own section.

This page is for people who know React but not its internals. It covers how fast use(store) is. If you haven't read how use(store) works, start there. It explains what a store is, what a reader is, and why every reader of a changed store re-renders.

All the data →

How each variant reads state: use(store) puts each entity in its own store, with small stores for the selection, the filter, the expanded rows, and the details. Redux and Zustand read one store with a selector per value. The granular control is Zustand with a store per entity, and store-single is one store without selectors. The code is in the code compared.

What each scenario does

The main suite is a list of rows with a selection, a filter with a count, and rows that can expand to show details. Each scenario makes one kind of update.

ScenarioThe updateWhat it isolates
Selection (selection)Select another rowEvery row reads the selection. Stores re-render every row and rely on the compiler, and selectors run in every row and re-render two.
Entity edit (entity)Change one row's dataA store per entity re-renders one row, and selector libraries run every row's selector.
Filter (filter)Change the filter textDerived data in every row, and a derived count.
Conditional read, inline (details-inline)Change details that a few expanded rows show in the row itselfA conditional use(store) against a selector that can't be conditional.
Conditional read, child component (details-component)The same, read in a child that only mounts when a row is expandedThe usual workaround for selectors.
Subscribe churn (details-churn)Expand every tenth row, then collapse themMounting and unmounting readers, plus every row reading the expanded state.
Add / remove (structure)Add a row, then remove itList updates. Every variant re-renders every row.

From the counting build at 1,000 rows, every component compiled: work for one update. Counted renders are the renders of Row, RowView, DetailsView, and CountView, not every component (App and the list aren't counted). Row renders are among them.

Why

In the inline conditional read, only expanded rows read the details store, so use(store) makes 30 counted renders and no selector calls. Redux renders as many, but makes 4,003 selector calls. On selection, it goes the other way. use(store) renders 1,000 rows, and Zustand renders 2.

Subscribe churn is new in this report. With use(store), every row reads the expanded-rows store, so every row re-renders (1,000 Row renders against 99 for Redux). A tenth of them also mount or unmount a details reader. It still matches or beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in every configuration: up to 1.5× faster (5 faster, 1 tie).

Controls: one store, no compiler, and Context

The granular control puts each entity in its own Zustand store, so it shows how much of the win comes from granularity alone. It isn't part of the headline.

One store holding everything, with no selectors, is the worst case for stores (store-single). With the compiler, it still beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in most configurations: 1.2× slower to 4.0× faster (26 faster, 9 tie, 7 slower).

Why, and the comparison with Context

With the compiler, a row whose output didn't change still runs, but it returns its cached element, so React skips everything below it. Without the compiler, use(store) loses badly where its rows re-render and the selector apps' rows don't: selection (7.7–13× slower) and subscribe churn (3.5–4.4× slower). Where every variant re-renders every row, in add / remove, it still wins.

Against Context, use(store) beats a context per slice in every configuration (1.1–11× faster). Against one context for everything, it's 1.1× slower to 9.3× faster (30 faster, 5 tie, 7 slower). It loses to one context only in these scenarios: filter and subscribe churn. There, the counting build shows the same renders for both, because every row reads the changed value either way. The biggest loss is 1.1× slower. A separate page compares use(store) and Context at each compiler setting.

Is Redux slow because of Redux Toolkit?

At 1,000 rows, against the fastest Redux setup in each configuration, use(store) matches or beats it in 14 of 14: 1.4–10× faster.

All the data →

How Redux Toolkit's defaults were checked

Redux Toolkit uses Immer, which freezes state by default. That's part of idiomatic Redux, so the main suite keeps it. The fairness controls check how much it costs. They run the main scenarios at 1,000 rows with a hand-written reducer (redux-plain) and with Immer's auto-freeze off (redux-nofreeze).

It does cost something. Against Redux Toolkit, the hand-written reducer is up to 1.4× faster (6 faster, 8 tie), and turning off auto-freeze is up to 1.3× faster (6 faster, 8 tie). This only moves the Redux column, because the faster of Redux and Zustand is Zustand in every main-suite configuration.

To check whether a leaner Redux changes any verdict, a second run timed use(store), Zustand, and all three Redux setups together, at 1,000 rows. Against Zustand in the same run, it's 1.1× slower to 4.4× faster (12 faster, 2 slower), the same selection losses as the main suite.

Selection: where it loses, and the fix

Selection is where use(store) loses, and that's the floor of a model without selectors, not a bug. A profile of two-store rows (below) puts the gap in running the component, not in the store. The fix is keyed selection, and it wins every configuration where it was measured.

At the largest size with a four times CPU slowdown, it's 1.4× faster. Against the granular control it loses at every size: up to 1.4× slower (1 tie, 5 slower).

All the data →

In the main suite, the store variant selects without keys: every Row reads the selected id. Here's one selection update at 1,000 rows, with no CPU slowdown. Zustand is shown at its faster compiler setting, which is the one the verdict uses.

VariantRow rendersSelector callsMedian ms per update
use(store) with the compiler1,00000.169
Zustand without the compiler (its faster setting here)24,0200.150
Redux with the compiler24,0030.250
The granular control with the compiler23,0140.119
Why

With use(store), every row re-renders, the compiler returns the cached RowView element for all but two of them, and the same-element bailout skips reconciling it. Zustand re-renders two rows, but it runs every row's selectors to find them. The verdict is 1.1× slower.

A CPU profile splits the cost per row. It was taken on the previous build, on the same case in the sweeps (below), where each row reads two stores. Visiting the row's fiber costs about the same either way, because Zustand's rows are cloned and bail out, and the store rows re-render and skip their children. The difference is the component itself. Running a compiled row, even one that returns its cached element, costs more than a couple of cheap selector calls. In that profile, removing all of the store's own work (the reads, comparing them, and marking readers) would only bring it to about a tie. Store-side trims measured on that build were too small to keep, so I reverted them. When each row reads only one or two values, I don't think a store-side optimization changes this.

The explainer covers the same case in when rows read only one or two values.

The fix: keyed selection

Instead of every row reading the selected id, each row reads a store that says whether it's selected. The stores are created on demand by weakMemo, the helper from shared derived data. Selecting a row updates the old row's store and the new row's store, so two rows re-render. It's the store version of a keyed selector, like Solid's createSelector, and the explainer has a sandbox for it.

The code 
function createApp(initialEntities) {  const entities = new Map();  for (const entity of addFields(initialEntities)) {    entities.set(entity.id, createStore(entity));  }  s = {    entities,    ids: createStore(initialEntities.map(e => e.id)),    selectedId: null,  };  selectedStoreFor = weakMemo(id => createStore(false));  const actions = {    editEntity(index) {      s.entities.get('e' + index).update(e => ({        ...e,        x: e.x + 1,      }));    },    select(index) {      const next = 'e' + index;      const prev = s.selectedId;      if (prev === next) {        return;      }      if (prev !== null) {        selectedStoreFor(prev).update(false);      }      selectedStoreFor(next).update(true);      s.selectedId = next;    },  };  return {    App,    actions,  };}

The id is a primitive, so weakMemo keeps these stores in a Map for as long as selectedStoreFor lives. The benchmark creates selectedStoreFor per mount. A row reads its own selection store:

function Row4({id}) {  const e = use(s.entities.get(id));  const selected = use(selectedStoreFor(id));  return (    <WideRowView      selected={selected}      label={e.label}      x={e.x}      y={e.y}    />  );}

All the data →

What the sweeps vary, and plain use(store)

The sweeps measure the hardest case for selection, rows that read only two stores: their entity and the selection. They vary two things at 1,000 rows. One is how much of the app the compiler covers (uncovered rows are 'use no memo' copies), and the other is how many props each row renders. They compare plain use(store), keyed selection (store-keyed), Redux, and Zustand.

  • Plain use(store) wins every entity configuration and loses every selection one. Fully compiled, it's 1.4× slower. With half the rows compiled it's 9.9–10.0× slower, and with no compiler it's 19× slower.

That's the cost of partial compiler coverage - a reader the compiler doesn't cover re-renders its children, unless you memoize them by hand. With keyed selection, coverage doesn't matter, because only two rows render.

Two design changes could close the gap for unkeyed selection, and neither is implemented. The compiler could emit a small check next to a component that says whether its output changes for new store values. React could then run the check instead of the component. Or React could re-run only the memoized blocks that depend on the changed reads. Both are changes to the compiler and the reconciler, not to the store.

Benchmarks ported from the Redux team's suite

In the ported Redux suites, plain use(store) loses only on derived selectors (6 configurations), and with weakMemo it wins those too.

  • Rapid dispatch (bursts of dispatches per task, including a Redux Toolkit listener cascade): 1.5–1.9× faster.
  • Many components reading the same counter: 1.2× faster.
  • A deep tree with nested Hooks and counters at the leaves: up to 2.2× faster (11 faster, 1 tie).
  • Derived selectors (components that share expensive derived data): plain use(store) is 1.1–1.4× slower. With the recommended pattern it's 1.3–1.5× faster. That one has its own section.
Where these benchmarks come from

I wrote the main suite for this experiment, so it could be built to favor stores. These four scenarios come from react-redux-benchmarks, which the Redux team maintains. The Redux variant keeps their code as written. The use(store) variants follow the explainer's patterns, and the Zustand variants follow Zustand's docs. Random numbers and timestamps are seeded so every variant renders the same thing, and each update is timed in flushSync.

Shared derived data: every reader computes it unless you share it

Plain use(store) computes shared derived data once per component that reads it. With weakMemo, it computes it once per snapshot and beats Redux in every configuration of the spike (below) that does any work: 1.4–1.9× faster.

The spike grows the readers per category. Plain use(store) falls further behind as they grow: 2.1–2.5× slower with fewer readers, and 3.6–4.5× slower with more. store-memo stays ahead of Redux (1.4–1.9× faster). The fastest correct sharing option in each configuration is 1.6–2.0× faster. That's a little ahead of store-memo, which is what you'd expect from taking the best of several. These ranges leave out the 4 role configurations, where nothing reads the update.

In the ported derived-selectors benchmark, plain use(store) is 1.1–1.4× slower against the fastest of Redux and Zustand. With weakMemo (store-memo) it's 1.3–1.5× faster. Neither count includes the 2 role configurations, which are unread updates with no work for any store variant.

Why every reader computes it, and the options

The problem: memoization is per component

Redux shares derived data with createSelector: the selector caches its result, and every component that uses it gets the same one. use(store) has no selectors. The compiler memoizes a derivation per component instance, so each reader computes it once per snapshot, and when the stores change, every reader computes it again.

The derived-selectors benchmark from react-redux-benchmarks shows this. Each category has 5 components that show stats computed from every post and comment. On a score update, Redux runs the expensive derivation an average of 58.1 times, and plain use(store) runs it 90 times. The spike raises that to 20 and 50 readers per category to see how the cost grows. With the most readers, a score update costs 450 derivations with plain use(store) and still 58.1 with Redux.

The constraint: correct under concurrency

Two things let a shared derivation stay correct under concurrency:

  • Store values are treated as immutable snapshots, like state. An update replaces the value, so a derivation cached by the identity of its inputs can't return a result computed from other data. Mutating a store value in place breaks this, the same as with useState.
  • Within a root, every component in a render reads every store at the same point and gets the same snapshot object. So every reader in a render hits the same cache entry, and a concurrent render at a different point uses different keys.

Computing the derived value in the update instead, and putting it in its own store, looks faster, but it tears (see no tearing in the explainer). The derivation runs on the latest values, not the ones a render reads. Take a pending transition on one store and an urgent update on another. The urgent commit shows stats that include the transition's data next to rows that don't. spike-shared-derived/concurrency.mjs reproduces it with the real reconciler. It's in the spike as store-derived, for reference only.

The options and what each costs

OptionCorrect under concurrencyWhat it costs
Derive in each component (plain use(store))YesThe shared work grows with the number of readers.
Compute in the update (store-derived)No, it tearsA mutable mirror of the latest values, and a second update in every action.
A userland memo keyed by snapshot identity (store-memo, store-reselect)YesOne line at module scope. Works today.
A React-provided client cache() (userland stand-ins: store-cache-render, store-cache-gen)YesNew client semantics for an existing API, and a lifetime to decide.
Sharing emitted by the compiler (a hand-edited stand-in: store-compiled-shared)YesThe compiler can't tell an expensive or shared call from a cheap one, so it needs a heuristic.
Derived stores (a userland stand-in: store-derived-lazy)YesThe most new API, and a derived store can't take a render-time argument.

Every option that shares computes the same number of derivations per update as createSelector (58 for store-memo on that score update), so the work doesn't separate them. Their timings differ a bit by configuration, and no option is fastest everywhere. Correctness, memory, and API cost do separate them.

The recommendation: weakMemo

Read the stores in render, then call a derivation wrapped in weakMemo. It caches by the identity of its arguments, with objects in a WeakMap and primitives in a Map under them, like cache() on the server. When a snapshot is replaced, its entries are collected with it.

The code 
function weakMemo(fn) {  const root = createNode();  return function () {    const node = getNode(root, arguments, 0);    if (node.hasValue) {      return node.value;    }    const value = fn.apply(null, arguments);    node.hasValue = true;    node.value = value;    return value;  };}

In the benchmark that's one line at module scope, const getSharedCategoryStats = weakMemo(getCategoryStats), and a call in render:

function CategoryStats({category}) {  const posts = use(s.posts);  const comments = use(s.comments);  const stats = getSharedCategoryStats(    posts,    comments,    category,  );  return (    <div>      {category}: {stats.postCount} posts, avg{' '}      {stats.avgScore.toFixed(1)}    </div>  );}
  • Read the stores in render and pass the snapshots to the shared function.
  • Put the snapshot arguments first, so primitives are keyed under an object that gets collected.
  • The compiler still memoizes the call per instance, so the shared cache is only checked when a snapshot changes.

The explainer has a sandbox for this pattern. How React itself should share derived data is still open. A client cache() scoped to a render is the leading option, and weakMemo is the userland version the benchmarks measure.

What the same-element bailout contributes

Over the 28 configurations the build without the same-element bailout measured, use(store) with the compiler matches or beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in 26 with the bailout, and in 24 without it.

  • It helps wherever every row re-renders: selection (up to 1.3× faster (3 faster, 1 tie)), subscribe churn (1.1–1.2× faster), and add / remove (1.2× faster). It changes 4 headline verdicts, two in selection and two in subscribe churn. These compare the run without it to the run with it, and the two runs weren't interleaved. Without it, selection is up to 1.4× slower (1 tie, 3 slower).
  • Keyed selection doesn't need it - it wins 14 of 14 selection sweeps without the bailout, the same as with it.
What the bailout is, and how this was measured

Every number above uses the same-element bailout (DCP-10). When a component returns the exact element it returned last time, React skips reconciling it. That's what the compiler's cached element hits on every row that didn't change. It's a reconciler change (not part of the store), and it runs for every function component. So it's behind its own flag, enableSameElementBailout, and it's the first PR in the use(store) stack.

To show what it contributes, the main suite at 1,000 and 10,000 rows and the sweeps also ran on the same build without it (react-builds/head-nobailout). These results aren't in the headline.

Selector libraries can avoid this with useDeferredValue, so the typing suite adds that version of each. It closes most of the gap. With the same slowdown, the p95 is 44.2 ms for use(store), 49.1 ms for Zustand with useDeferredValue, and 61.1 ms for Redux with it. The difference is that use(store) gets this from startTransition, the same as useState, without a deferred copy of the value.

How typing was measured

This benchmark types 19 keys into the filter while 10,000 expensive rows re-filter. Every variant updates the input right away and the list in a transition. A store update in a transition is a transition update, so React can interrupt the list render to handle the next key. Redux and Zustand read through useSyncExternalStore, which renders synchronously even inside a transition, so the list blocks the input.

Latency is keydown to the next frame, over every key of every run.

This measures how much the heap grows when the rows mount, after garbage collection, divided by the row count. With the compiler at the largest size, use(store) uses 2,901 bytes per row, against 4,549 for Zustand and 7,191 for Redux. One context uses the least, 2,167. A store per entity costs more than one context, and less than either Redux or Zustand. Mounting takes 51.8 ms with use(store) and 97.4 ms with Redux.

Where it doesn't win

I count the headline, the granular control, the ported suites, the fairness run against Redux, the sweeps, and the spike as results. Across them, the store side loses 41 of 224. The controls (one store, no compiler, Context, and no bailout) have their own sections and aren't counted here. For shared derived data, the recommended pattern wins in the same configurations. For selection, keyed selection wins every sweep, but it wasn't timed in the main suite or against the granular control:

  • Main suite against the faster of Redux and Zustand: 3 of 42, all selection. Keyed selection is the pattern for this, but it isn't timed in the main suite (see selection).
  • Main suite against the granular control: 6 of 42, all but one of them selection. Keyed selection is the pattern for this too, but it isn't timed against the granular control. The exception is subscribe churn at the smallest size, where every row reads the expanded-rows store. A keyed store per row for the expanded state would apply the same fix, but it isn't measured.
  • The ported Redux benchmarks: 6 of 38, all derived selectors with plain use(store). With weakMemo it wins 6 of 6 (see shared derived data).
  • The fairness run against the fastest Redux setup: 0 of 14.
  • The sweeps: 14 of 56, all selection with plain use(store). Keyed selection wins all of them.
  • The shared-derived-data spike: 12 of 32, all with plain use(store). With weakMemo it wins 12 of 12.

Every comparison the store side loses, with what the counting build says each side did for one update of that scenario. A tie is a difference in means within two standard errors. A larger difference is a win or a loss only if every browser restart agrees on the direction (the side that is faster in the pooled means is faster in each restart, restarts paired by restart number). Otherwise it is a tie. Verdicts compare means, which include the slow tail: where a median is lower but the mean is higher, the store side has more slow updates.

The variants differ only in how they read state

The code below is pulled from the measured benchmark sources when this page is built, with the counting instrumentation removed. Every variant renders the same RowView and CountView components, so the DOM is the same in all of them. The explainer's what re-renders demo runs a list like this one with selectors and with use(store), and counts the renders and selector calls.

use(store)

Each entity has its own store, and there are small stores for the selection, the filter, the expanded rows, and the details. A row reads four stores. It reads the details store only when it's expanded, so rows that aren't expanded don't subscribe to it.

The code 
function Row({id}) {  const entity = use(s.entities.get(id));  const selected = use(s.selected) === id;↑ every row reads the selection  const matches = matchesFilter(entity.label, use(s.filter));  const expanded = use(s.expanded).has(id);  let details = null;  let children = null;  if (expanded) {    if (s.detailsMode === 'component') {      children = <Details />;    } else {      // Read conditionally: rows that aren't expanded don't subscribe.      details = use(s.details);↑ only expanded rows subscribe    }  }  return (    <RowView      label={entity.label}      x={entity.x}      y={entity.y}      color={entity.color}      selected={selected}      matches={matches}      details={details}>      {children}    </RowView>  );}

Redux

Redux Toolkit's createSlice, read with react-redux's useSelector. The selectors are inline, and the count uses createSelector. Every row runs four selectors on every update.

The code 
function Row({id}) {  const entity = useSelector(s => s.entities[id]);  const selected = useSelector(s => s.selected === id);↑ runs in every row on every update  const matches = useSelector(s =>    matchesFilter(s.entities[id].label, s.filter),  );  const expanded = useSelector(s => s.expanded[id] === true);  return (    <RowView      label={entity.label}      x={entity.x}      y={entity.y}      color={entity.color}      selected={selected}      matches={matches}      details={null}>      {expanded ? <Details /> : null}    </RowView>  );}

Zustand

Zustand uses one create() store with a selector per value.

The code 
function Row({id}) {  const entity = useBench(s => s.entities[id]);  const selected = useBench(s => s.selected === id);  const matches = useBench(s =>    matchesFilter(s.entities[id].label, s.filter),  );  const expanded = useBench(s => s.expanded[id] === true);  return (    <RowView      label={entity.label}      x={entity.x}      y={entity.y}      color={entity.color}      selected={selected}      matches={matches}      details={null}>      {expanded ? <Details /> : null}    </RowView>  );}

The count is computed in render from two selectors.

The code 
function Count() {  const labels = useBench(s => s.labels);  const filter = useBench(s => s.filter);  let count = 0;  for (let i = 0; i < labels.length; i++) {    if (matchesFilter(labels[i], filter)) {      count++;    }  }  return <CountView count={count} />;}

The granular control

The same as Zustand, but each entity is its own Zustand store. Editing an entity notifies only that entity's subscribers. I think it's the closest selector-based match for a store per entity, so it separates what granularity buys from what the store implementation buys.

The code 
function Row({id}) {  const entity = useStore(box.entities.get(id), selectEntity);↑ this entity's own store  const selected = useShared(s => s.selected === id);  const matches = useShared(s =>    matchesFilter(entity.label, s.filter),  );  const expanded = useShared(s => s.expanded[id] === true);  return (    <RowView      label={entity.label}      x={entity.x}      y={entity.y}      color={entity.color}      selected={selected}      matches={matches}      details={null}>      {expanded ? <Details /> : null}    </RowView>  );}

The compiled Row

This is the store Row after the React Compiler (compiler build c59ecf06d45b47db, the one the benchmarks used). The reads run on every render. The element is cached, so when a row's inputs didn't change, it returns the same RowView element it returned last time.

The code 
function Row(t0) {  const $ = _c(15);  const {id} = t0;  let t1;  if ($[0] !== id) {    t1 = s.entities.get(id);    $[0] = id;    $[1] = t1;  } else {    t1 = $[1];  }  const entity = use(t1);  const selected = use(s.selected) === id;↑ the reads run on every render  const t2 = entity.label;  const t3 = use(s.filter);  let t4;  if ($[2] !== entity.label || $[3] !== t3) {    t4 = matchesFilter(t2, t3);    $[2] = entity.label;    $[3] = t3;    $[4] = t4;  } else {    t4 = $[4];  }  const matches = t4;  const expanded = use(s.expanded).has(id);  let details = null;  let children = null;  if (expanded) {    if (s.detailsMode === 'component') {      let t5;      if ($[5] === Symbol.for('react.memo_cache_sentinel')) {        t5 = <Details />;        $[5] = t5;      } else {        t5 = $[5];      }      children = t5;    } else {      details = use(s.details);    }  }  let t5;  if (    $[6] !== children ||    $[7] !== details ||    $[8] !== entity.color ||    $[9] !== entity.label ||    $[10] !== entity.x ||    $[11] !== entity.y ||    $[12] !== matches ||    $[13] !== selected↑ changes in two rows when the selection moves  ) {    t5 = (      <RowView        label={entity.label}        x={entity.x}        y={entity.y}        color={entity.color}        selected={selected}        matches={matches}        details={details}>        {children}      </RowView>    );    $[6] = children;    $[7] = details;    $[8] = entity.color;    $[9] = entity.label;    $[10] = entity.x;    $[11] = entity.y;    $[12] = matches;    $[13] = selected;    $[14] = t5;  } else {    t5 = $[14];↑ returns the cached element, so RowView is skipped  }  return t5;}

Caveats

  • These are synthetic benchmarks. Each app is small and built to isolate one thing. There's no data from a real app yet.
  • Every result is from one machine and one browser. Whether the ratios carry over to other machines isn't tested.
  • Updates are timed inside flushSync, so they measure synchronous work. Only the typing benchmark measures what transitions do for responsiveness.
  • The wins depend on the React Compiler. Without it, use(store) loses wherever its readers re-render and the selector apps' don't (see the controls). In a partly compiled app, a reader the compiler doesn't cover re-renders its children.
  • Selection and subscribe churn in the main suite depend on the same-element bailout, which is its own PR, the first in the use(store) stack.
  • The use(store) variants follow the explainer's patterns, and the selector variants follow their libraries' docs. A selector app tuned by hand (for example, with a store per entity) does better, which is why the granular control has its own column.
  • The compiler doesn't memoize a value built across use() calls, because it flattens the scope that contains use(). Examples are an array filled with push(use(a)) or a loop that reads stores. A call on values read with use() is memoized.
  • The headline compares against idiomatic Redux Toolkit, and leaner Redux setups are faster in some configurations. The run that compares them with use(store) covers only 1,000 rows. There, no verdict flips (14 of 14), but the other sizes aren't measured with leaner Redux.
  • The typing and memory benchmarks have far fewer samples than the main suite: 19 keys per typing run and one measurement per memory run, over 3 runs. Each table shows how many runs.

How the numbers were measured

The build

Every benchmark result on this page comes from one frozen React build: React 0.0.0-experimental-a3d8e745-20261101 (react-builds/head) as production bundles, with compiler build c59ecf06d45b47db. The exception is the section without the same-element bailout, which uses the same commit with only that flag off. Each result file records the build it ran on, and this page's number check fails if any pinned file came from a different one. The libraries are Redux 5.0.1, react-redux 9.3.1, Redux Toolkit 2.13.0, Zustand 5.0.16, and Reselect 5.3.0. The browser is Chrome's headless shell 145.0.7632.6 on an Apple M4 Max, driven by Playwright from Node v25.4.0.

Timing and the ambient CPU gate

Each update is timed as one browser task inside flushSync, so every library renders synchronously and the selector work during dispatch is counted. The main suite has 42 configurations: seven scenarios, at 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 rows, with a 1× and 4× CPU slowdown. Each configuration gets 50 warm-up updates and then 200 timed ones, with the order shuffled. Each configuration runs in 3 browser restarts, except selection at 1× CPU and subscribe churn at 1× CPU (5 restarts, every size). Those got extra restarts because their first three disagreed close to parity, and two of the three headline losses are in them. The rule that every restart must agree (see how a win is decided) applies to all of their restarts. That's 386,400 timed updates in the main suite.

Other work on the machine slows a benchmark down. So timing ran in small units behind a gate on ambient CPU, the cores used by processes outside the benchmark's own process tree. A unit started only when ambient CPU was at or below 3.5 cores. It was thrown away and re-run if the mean during the unit was above 4.5. The frozen build has 100 timing units. Ambient CPU is logged for every unit that ran under this gate, 86 of them. Across those, the mean ambient CPU per unit was 2.05 cores at the median and 3.49 at most.

The load-average gate it replaced

It replaced a gate on the load average. Load includes the benchmark's own work, so that gate held back and threw away units because of the benchmark itself. Only the first restart of the main suite ran under it (14 units). Every other restart and benchmark ran under the ambient gate.

How a win is decided

Verdicts compare average times. Differences within two standard errors are ties. Anything bigger counts as a win or a loss only if every browser restart agrees on which side is faster, and otherwise it's a tie too. A verdict like 1.4× faster means the other side's average time is that many times longer. The tables also show medians and spreads. A median can be lower on the side that's slower overall, when that side has more slow updates.

Each library is compared at its own faster compiler setting. So "the faster of Redux and Zustand" can be Zustand without the compiler in one configuration, and with it in the next.

Redux in the headline is idiomatic Redux, the setup the react-redux docs recommend: Redux Toolkit's configureStore and createSlice, with Immer's auto-freeze on, read through react-redux. Two leaner setups (a hand-written reducer, and auto-freeze off) are timed against it in the fairness controls. Even against the fastest of the three in each configuration, at 1,000 rows, use(store) matches or beats Redux in 14 of 14.

The counting build: what each update did

The counting build is a second build of the same code with counters. It counts renders of Row, RowView, DetailsView, and CountView, not every component, with Row renders counted on their own too. It also counts selector calls and runs of an expensive derivation. It's deterministic, so it isn't timed or gated. Before any timing, each scenario replays 20 updates in every variant, and the DOM must match after each one. That check runs in jsdom and in Chrome, except for the sweeps, which run it in Chrome only.

Notes for reading the scenarios

  • Add / remove (structure) is low-signal. Every variant re-renders every row, because the list's elements are new, so it mostly measures list reconciliation.
  • In the shared-derived-data benchmarks, a role update changes a user's role, and nothing renders users. The DOM never changes. use(store) does nothing for it, and those configurations are counted as "no work" instead of as a win.

The headline is lower than the last report's

On the last report's final build, use(store) matched or beat the faster of Redux and Zustand in 36 of 36 configurations. Two things changed since then. A review of the benchmark code found and fixed two places that were unfair to the selector libraries, and the React build changed too (the HostRoot redesign). By inspection, the fixes are the likely main cause, but neither change was isolated. The fixes:

  • The selector apps' rows had an extra selector for inline details in every scenario, even where the details are read in a child component. Now only the inline-details scenario uses a row with that selector.
  • Zustand computed the filter count in a selector, so the loop over every label ran on every update. Now it selects the labels and the filter and counts in render, like the other variants.

Both fixes remove work that only the selector apps were doing. Neither was timed on its own. The review also added the subscribe churn scenario, which mounts and unmounts readers. The fairer comparison is the one I stand behind, so it's the headline now.

How to reproduce

Everything runs from fixtures/store-bench. Install the libraries there first with yarn (they aren't part of the React repo).

  • ./run-report-matrix.sh runs every benchmark this page cites on the frozen build in react-builds/head. It builds the bundles, checks that every variant renders the same DOM, runs the counting build, and then times small units that it can resume. MATRIX=nobailout runs the build without the same-element bailout. EXTRA_SUITES='fairness5:fairness|--n=1000 --throttle=1,4 --iterations=200 --warmup=50' adds the leaner-Redux run, and RESTARTS=5 RESTART_FROM=4 ONLY='-(selection|details-churn)-x1$' adds the extra restarts.
  • ambient-cpu.mjs is the gate. It reports the CPU used by processes outside the benchmark's own process tree. The script waits for it before each unit, samples it during the unit, and logs it per unit.
  • node report-data.mjs computes every number on this page from the result files pinned in results/report-sources.json, and writes docs/use-store/data/bench-data.json. --check fails if regenerating would change anything.
  • node docs/use-store/tools/build-docs.mjs --pages=benchmark-report, from the repo root, builds this page from docs/use-store/src/benchmark-report.src.html. tools/check-docs.mjs runs the checks, including the one that fails on any digit in the prose that isn't generated.

The full matrix takes hours. Run it on a quiet machine, plugged in, with nothing heavy alongside.
